'''''Polypodium vulgare''''', the '''common polypody''', is an evergreen fern of the family [[Polypodiaceae]]. The name is derived from Greek ''poly-'' ("many") and ''pous, podos'' ("foot"). Polypody has traditional uses in cooking for its aroma and sweet taste, and in herbal medicine as a purgative and vermifuge. This species is expansive and highly adapted to many environments. 

==Description==
''Polypodium vulgare'', also known as common polypody, is a fern developing isolated fronds along a horizontal [[rhizome]]. The fronds, with triangular leaflets, measure {{convert|10|to|50|cm}}.{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}} They grow apart from each other and are divided all the way back to the central stem in 10 to 18 pairs of segments or [[leaflet (botany)|leaflet]]s which measure {{Convert|10-20|cm|in}} long and {{Convert|5-7|cm|in}} wide<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025 |title=WFO (2025): Polypodium vulgare L |url=https://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0001107395#C |access-date=14 Mar 2025 |website=World Flora Online}}</ref>

The leaflets become much shorter at the end of the frond. The leaflets are generally whole or slightly denticulated and somewhat wider at their base, where they often touch each other. They have an alternating arrangement, those on one side being slightly offset from those on the other side. The [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]s have no scales.

The [[sorus|sori]] are found on the lower side of the fronds and range in colour from bright yellow to orange. They became dark grey at maturity<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Manning |first=John |title=The Core Cape flora |last2=Goldblatt |first2=Peter |last3=Manning |first3=John |date=2012 |publisher=SANBI |isbn=978-1-919976-74-7 |series=Plants of the Greater Cape floristic region / John Manning and Peter Goldblatt |location=Pretoria}}</ref>

*Period of sporulation: July to September.
*Mode of dissemination: [[anemochory]] (wind dispersal){{Citation needed|date=March 2025}}

==Distribution and habitat==
The common polypody occurs throughout western Europe and North Africa.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Map |url=http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/orm/polypodia/polyp/polyvulv.jpg |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020222233319/http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/orm/polypodia/polyp/polyvulv.jpg |archive-date=2002-02-22 |website=linnaeus.nrm.se}}</ref> In Britain and Ireland, it is widespread in all areas except the drier parts of eastern England, and is most abundant in the high humidity of the uplands in the west and north; it occurs from sea level up to 760 m altitude.<ref name="BSBI">{{cite web | title=Polypody ''Polypodium vulgare'' L. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.bvd | access-date=2024-12-07}}</ref> It is very common in [[France]], where it is found up to an altitude of {{convert|2000|m}}.{{citation needed|date=May 2015}} It is also quite common in [[Scandinavia]] and [[Carpathian Mountains]]. It is an [[introduced species]] in [[New Zealand]] that has begun to spread into the wild as an [[invasive species]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/sfc340.pdf/|title=Invasive weeds|website=[[Department of Conservation (New Zealand)|Department of Conservation]]|access-date=8 March 2025}}</ref>

===Habitat===
''Polypodium vulgare'' is a hardy and highly adaptable species which commonly lives in the [[Temperate climate|northern temperate zone]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Haufler |first1=Christopher H. |last2=Windham |first2=Michael D. |last3=Rabe |first3=Eric W. |date=April 1995 |title=Reticulate Evolution in the Polypodium vulgare Complex |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2419442 |journal=Systematic Botany |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=89 |doi=10.2307/2419442|jstor=2419442 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> This fern is found in shaded and semi-shaded locations. It is a [[lithophyte]] (grows on rocks), and is found growing in the moss on old walls, cliffs, cracks in rocks, and in rocky undergrowth; also as an [[epiphyte]] on mossy trees.<ref name=":2" /> Its evergreen leaves allow for the absorption of sunlight during seasons when light is scarce; this is an evolutionary advantage in [[Deciduous|deciduous forests]].{{cn|date=December 2024}}

This species can grow as an epiphyte regardless of the height or branching of the tree it occupies. ''Polypodium vulgare'' benefits the most from this relationship if it can grow in the crotch of a tree with forking branches, leading to greater water, sunlight, and mineral collection. This species can equally achieve maturity as an epiphyte or on the ground.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Johnson |first=Duncan S. |date=October 1921 |title=Polypodium vulgare as an Epiphyte |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/332920 |journal=Botanical Gazette |language=en |volume=72 |issue=4 |pages=237–244 |doi=10.1086/332920 |issn=0006-8071}}</ref>

==Origins==
''Polypodium vulgare'' is an [[Polyploid|allotetraploid]] species, believed to have arisen by chromosome doubling of a sterile diploid [[hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] between two ferns which are not known in Europe. The fern's proposed parents are the northern Asian and northern North American ''Polypodium sibiricum'' and western North American ''[[Polypodium glycyrrhiza]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Reticulate Evolution in the Polypodium vulgare Complex|author=Haufler, Christopher H.|author2=Windham, Michael D.|author3=Rabe, Eric W.|journal=Systematic Botany|volume=20|issue=2|year=1995|pages=89–109|doi=10.2307/2419442|jstor=2419442}}</ref> Biochemical data point to a species from eastern [[Asia]] as the second possible parent. The genetics of this hybridisation caused ''Polypodium'' ''vulgare'' only to form [[Sporangium|sporangia]] in the sori of the [[Polyploidy|allotetraploid]]. This trait is dominant in the species ''[[Polypodium glycyrrhiza]]''.<ref name=":0" />

The specific traits likely appeared during the [[ice age]]. This restriction of [[habitat]] and the unique hybridisation led to its formation. As the ice melted, ''Polypodium vulgare'' was left to inhabit areas that once contained [[glacier]]s.<ref name=":0" />

== Identification ==
''Polypodium vulgare'' is a complex and unique species, making its [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomic classification]] and identification challenging. Subtle variations between different species of ''Polypodium'' muddle the process even further.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=January 2010 |title=Erratum |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.3120/0024-9637-57.1.75 |journal=Madroño |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=75–75 |doi=10.3120/0024-9637-57.1.75 |issn=0024-9637|url-access=subscription }}</ref> ''Polypodium vulgare'' inhabits [[Northern Europe]] and parts of Asia. There are only four [[Clade|clades]] included in this [[species]] that still exist. There was likely a significant divergence within the species ''Polypodium vulgare'' due to geographic isolation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sigel |first=Erin M. |last2=Windham |first2=Michael D. |last3=Haufler |first3=Christopher H. |last4=Pryer |first4=Kathleen M. |date=2014-10-01 |title=Phylogeny, Divergence Time Estimates, and Phylogeography of the Diploid Species of the Polypodium vulgare Complex (Polypodiaceae) |url=https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/aspt/sb/2014/00000039/00000004/art00003;jsessionid=62vdb8hestb82.x-ic-live-02 |journal=Systematic Botany |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=1042–1055 |doi=10.1600/036364414X683921|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Recognition of its leathery-textured [[Frond|fronds]], circular sori, and "lateral veins forked three to four times" <ref name=":1">{{Cite book |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/(issn)1095-8339a |title=Journal of the Linnean Society of London, Botany |publisher=Oxford University Press (OUP)}}</ref> are vital to identifying this species. Out of the genus ''[[Polypodium]]'', ''Polypodium vulgare'' has the most northern range. <ref name=":1" /> The combination of these common traits allow for the identification of this species.{{cn|date=December 2024}}

==Uses==
In cooking, the rhizome has a bittersweet taste. It has traditionally been used in some confectionery, such as [[nougat]], for its aromatic properties. In 1971, a [[saponin]], [[osladin]] was found in the roots and believed to be the compound responsible for the sweet taste as it elicits a relative sweetness 500 times sweeter than [[sucrose|sugar]] (by weight).<ref>{{in lang|en}} J Jizba, L Dolejs, V Herout & F Sorm, "The structure of osladin — The sweet principle of the rhizomes of Polypodium vulgare L.", in Tetrahedron Lett., vol. 18, 1971, p. 1329-1332. {{doi|10.1016/S0040-4039(01)96701-2}}.</ref>

The dried rhizome is used in [[herbal medicine]] as a [[purgative]] and [[vermifuge]]; these properties are due to the [[phytoecdysteroid]]s in the rhizome.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Camps, F.|author2=Claveria, E.|author3=Coll, J.|author4=Marco, M. P.|author5=Messeguer, J.|author6=Mela, E.|title=Ecdysteroid production in tissue cultures of Polypodium vulgare|journal= Phytochemistry|volume=29|issue=12|pages=3819|year=1990|doi=10.1016/0031-9422(90)85339-H|bibcode=1990PChem..29.3819C }}</ref> Its use as an herbal remedy has led this species to be recognised by the [[European Medicines Agency]]. The fronds contain compounds that aid in the healing of wounds and help to fight age-related diseases. These compounds include [[Phenolic acid|phenolic acids]] and [[Flavonoid|flavonoids]], which speed up the [[Regeneration (biology)|regeneration]] of cells. <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Farràs |first1=Adrià |last2=Mitjans |first2=Montserrat |last3=Maggi |first3=Filippo |last4=Caprioli |first4=Giovanni |last5=Vinardell |first5=María Pilar |last6=López |first6=Víctor |date=2021-09-16 |title=Polypodium vulgare L. (Polypodiaceae) as a Source of Bioactive Compounds: Polyphenolic Profile, Cytotoxicity and Cytoprotective Properties in Different Cell Lines |journal=Frontiers in Pharmacology |volume=12 |doi=10.3389/fphar.2021.727528 |doi-access=free |pmid=34603041 |pmc=8482143 |issn=1663-9812}}</ref>

===Research===
''P. vulgare'' plays the primary role in understanding of plant [[stomata]] responses to humidity. The Otto Lange group at the [[University of Würzburg]] first showed that stomatal opening and closing was performed in response to environmental humidity with Lange et al. 1971,<ref name="Mooney-1999">{{cite journal | last=Mooney | first=H. A. | title=On the Road to Global Ecology | journal=[[Annual Review of Energy and the Environment]] | publisher=[[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews]] | volume=24 | issue=1 | year=1999 | issn=1056-3466 | doi=10.1146/annurev.energy.24.1.1 | pages=1–31| doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Raschke-1975">{{cite journal | last=Raschke | first=K | title=Stomatal Action | journal=[[Annual Review of Plant Physiology]] | publisher=[[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews]] | volume=26 | issue=1 | year=1975 | issn=0066-4294 | doi=10.1146/annurev.pp.26.060175.001521 | pages=309–340}}</ref> and continued to use it to further illuminate stomatal-humidity responses in stomata-humidity-temperature dynamics in Lösch 1977 & 1979,<ref name="Berry-Bjorkman-1980">{{cite journal | last1=Berry | first1=J | last2=Bjorkman | first2=O | title=Photosynthetic Response and Adaptation to Temperature in Higher Plants | journal=[[Annual Review of Plant Physiology]] | publisher=[[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews]] | volume=31 | issue=1 | year=1980 | issn=0066-4294 | doi=10.1146/annurev.pp.31.060180.002423 | pages=491–543}}</ref> and metabolic energy supply to fuel stomatal articulation in Lösch & Tenhunen 1981.<ref name="Zeiger-1983">{{cite journal | last=Zeiger | first=E | title=The Biology of Stomatal Guard Cells | journal=[[Annual Review of Plant Physiology]] | publisher=[[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews]] | volume=34 | issue=1 | year=1983 | issn=0066-4294 | doi=10.1146/annurev.pp.34.060183.002301 | pages=441–474}}</ref>

==Note==
*The name ''Polypodium vulgare'' is sometimes applied to the ''[[Polypodium virginianum]]'' (rock polypody).{{cn|date=December 2024}}
